drafted_by: AI, requires clinician review before any real use.

questions.text: What is the skin problem: a rash, itch, bump, mole, wound, blisters, or something else? Where is it?
questions.rationale: Clarifying the main skin complaint guides the next branch of the interview.

questions.text: When did it start, and is it getting better, worse, or staying the same?
questions.rationale: Onset and course separate acute reactions from chronic conditions.

questions.text: Where did it begin, and has it spread to other areas?
questions.rationale: Distribution and spread are key to rash diagnosis.

questions.text: What does it look like: flat or raised, red, scaly, blistered, weeping, or crusted?
questions.rationale: Morphology narrows the dermatologic differential.

questions.text: Is it itchy, painful, burning, or numb?
questions.rationale: Itch versus pain separates eczema, urticaria, and shingles.

questions.text: Do you have fever or feel generally unwell?
questions.rationale: Systemic illness raises concern for serious infection or drug reaction.

questions.text: Is a red, warm, swollen area spreading, or are there red streaks?
questions.rationale: This suggests cellulitis or lymphangitis.

questions.text: Do you have blisters, peeling skin, or sores in your mouth, eyes, or genitals?
questions.rationale: Mucosal involvement suggests SJS/TEN or pemphigus.

questions.text: Have you started any new medicine, supplement, or antibiotic in the past few weeks?
questions.rationale: Drug reactions typically appear days to weeks after starting a new medicine.

questions.text: Do you have hives, swelling of the lips, tongue, or face, or trouble breathing?
questions.rationale: Urticaria with angioedema or breathing difficulty can be anaphylaxis.

questions.text: Is the rash purple or red spots that do not fade when you press on them, especially with fever?
questions.rationale: Non-blanching rash with fever may indicate meningococcemia or vasculitis.

questions.text: Is there a painful blistering rash on one side of your body, face, or near your eye?
questions.rationale: This suggests herpes zoster, and eye involvement is sight-threatening.

questions.text: Has a mole or spot changed in size, shape, color, or started to bleed or itch?
questions.rationale: Changes in a pigmented lesion raise concern for melanoma.

questions.text: Do you have a sore or wound that has not healed in several weeks?
questions.rationale: Non-healing lesions may be skin cancer, venous or diabetic ulcers, or infection.

questions.text: Have you used new soaps, cosmetics, detergents, plants, jewelry, or other products?
questions.rationale: Contact dermatitis is triggered by new exposures.

questions.text: Does anyone around you have a similar rash, lice, scabies, or cold sores?
questions.rationale: Close contact spread suggests scabies, impetigo, or viral infection.

questions.text: Have you been in tall grass or woods, been bitten by a tick or insect, or had a lot of sun exposure?
questions.rationale: These exposures raise risk of Lyme disease, rickettsial infection, and photosensitivity.

questions.text: Do you have eczema, asthma, hay fever, or food or drug allergies?
questions.rationale: Atopic history supports eczema or allergic causes.

questions.text: Have you had skin conditions or skin cancer before, or does anyone in your family?
questions.rationale: Personal and family history shape risk and likely diagnosis.

questions.text: Do you have diabetes, poor circulation, or a weakened immune system?
questions.rationale: These conditions increase risk of severe skin infection and slow healing.

questions.text: Is pregnancy possible right now?
questions.rationale: Pregnancy affects rash differential and safe treatment choices.

questions.text: What creams, medicines, or home remedies have you tried, and did they help?
questions.rationale: Treatment response and prior steroid use alter appearance and next steps.

questions.text: Does your work or hobbies involve chemicals, water, gloves, or animals?
questions.rationale: Occupational exposures cause contact dermatitis and zoonotic infections.

questions.text: What is the main thing you are worried this could be?
questions.rationale: Understanding the patient's concern guides reassurance and follow-up questions.

red_flags.label: Rapidly spreading redness with fever
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient describe a red, warm, swollen area that is spreading quickly, with red streaks or fever?

red_flags.label: Blisters or peeling with mucosal involvement
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report blisters, peeling skin, or sores in the mouth, eyes, or genitals, especially after a new medicine?

red_flags.label: Hives or swelling with breathing difficulty
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report hives, facial or tongue swelling, or trouble breathing?

red_flags.label: Non-blanching rash with fever
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient describe purple or red spots that do not fade with pressure, with fever or feeling very ill?

red_flags.label: Painful blistering rash near the eye
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report a painful one-sided blistering rash on the face or near the eye?

red_flags.label: Changing or bleeding mole
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report a mole or spot that has changed in size, shape, or color, or bleeds?

red_flags.label: Non-healing wound
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report a sore that has not healed in weeks, especially with diabetes or poor circulation?
